q-nn-count.label: Nouns that take no 'a' and no plural
q-nn-count.summary: Information, advice, furniture, luggage, machinery, scenery and poetry have no plural in -s.

q-nn-number.label: Singular-looking plurals and plural-looking singulars
q-nn-number.summary: News, physics and mathematics are singular; scissors, trousers and premises are plural.

q-nn-poss.label: The apostrophe and the of-form
q-nn-poss.summary: People and time take 's; lifeless things usually take 'of'.

q-nn-foreign.label: Latin and Greek plurals (criterion, datum, crisis)
q-nn-foreign.summary: Words borrowed from Latin and Greek keep their own plural pattern: criterion/criteria, datum/data, crisis/crises, analysis/analyses, radius/radii.

q-nn-doublemeaning.label: Brother/brethren, cloth/cloths, index/indices
q-nn-doublemeaning.summary: A handful of nouns have two different plural (or related) forms, each tied to a different meaning: brothers (sons of the same parents) vs brethren (members of a group), cloths (pieces of cloth) vs clothes (garments).

rules.text: These have no plural and take no 'a': information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, machinery, scenery, poetry, stationery, work, bread, traffic. Count them with a phrase: a piece of advice, an item of furniture.
rules.ok: He gave me some useful information.
rules.bad: He gave me some useful informations.

rules.text: Singular although they end in -s: news, physics, mathematics, economics, politics, measles, innings. Plural with no singular: scissors, trousers, spectacles, premises, proceeds, alms, tidings.
rules.ok: The news is good. These scissors are blunt.
rules.bad: The news are good. This scissor is blunt.

rules.text: After a number, a noun of measure stays singular when it is used as an adjective: a five-year plan, a ten-rupee note, two dozen eggs. Standing alone it takes the plural: the plan runs for five years.
rules.ok: He bought a ten-rupee note and two dozen eggs.
rules.bad: He bought a ten-rupees note and two dozens eggs.

rules.text: Use 's for people, animals, time and personified things: the boy's bag, a day's work, India's exports. Use 'of' for lifeless things: the leg of the table, the roof of the house.
rules.ok: A day's work; the roof of the house.
rules.bad: A day work; the house's roof.

rules.text: A plural ending in -s takes only the apostrophe: the boys' hostel. A plural not ending in -s takes 's: the children's park. For two owners of one thing, mark the last name only: Ram and Shyam's shop.
rules.ok: The boys' hostel; the children's park.
rules.bad: The boys's hostel; the childrens park.

rules.text: Words taken from Latin or Greek often keep their own plural rather than adding -s: criterion/criteria, phenomenon/phenomena, datum/data, memorandum/memoranda, analysis/analyses, crisis/crises, basis/bases, thesis/theses, hypothesis/hypotheses, radius/radii, syllabus/syllabi. 'Criterions' and 'phenomenons' are common mistakes.
rules.ok: Honesty is one criterion; hard work and punctuality are two more criteria.
rules.bad: Honesty is one of the criterions for selection.

rules.text: A few nouns carry two different forms for two different meanings: brothers (sons of the same parents) vs brethren (members of a society or community); cloths (pieces or kinds of fabric) vs clothes (garments worn); indexes (tables of contents) vs indices (signs used in algebra or statistics); dies (stamps used for printing/coining) vs dice (the small cubes used in games).
rules.ok: The reading room keeps old cloths for cleaning; the tailor sells clothes.

q-nn-count.cue: advice, information, furniture, luggage or scenery with an -s or an 'a' in front of it.
q-nn-count.standard: Ask whether the noun can be counted one by one. If it cannot, strip the -s and the 'a'.
q-nn-count.eliminate: Cross out any option that pluralises one of the listed nouns.
traps: 'Many informations' and 'two advices', which are normal in Indian English.
'A work' for a job: use 'a piece of work' or 'a job'.

q-nn-number.cue: news, physics, mathematics, scissors, trousers or premises as the subject.
q-nn-number.standard: Decide the noun's real number from the list, then match the verb to it.
q-nn-number.fast: Ends in -s but names one subject or one thing: singular.
q-nn-number.eliminate: Drop options that treat 'news' or 'mathematics' as plural.
traps: 'A scissor' and 'a trouser' for one object: say 'a pair of'.
A measure noun pluralised before another noun: 'a five-years plan'.

q-nn-poss.cue: An apostrophe, or a choice between 's and an of-phrase.
q-nn-poss.standard: Ask whether the owner is living or a stretch of time. If it is, use 's; otherwise use 'of'.
q-nn-poss.fast: Living or time, use 's. Lifeless, use 'of'.
q-nn-poss.eliminate: Remove 's on a plural that already ends in -s, and 'of' on a person.
traps: 'The table's leg' for a lifeless thing.
'A day work' with the apostrophe dropped.

q-nn-foreign.cue: A noun ending in -on, -is, -um or -us, used with a count ('one of the ...', 'several ...').
q-nn-foreign.standard: Recall the word's own borrowed plural rather than adding an ordinary -s.
q-nn-foreign.eliminate: Drop any option that adds a plain -s to one of these borrowed nouns.
traps: 'Criterions' and 'phenomenons' sound like ordinary English plurals and are the commonest wrong answers.

q-nn-doublemeaning.cue: brother(s), cloth(s), index(es) or die/dice, where the sentence's meaning decides which form fits.
q-nn-doublemeaning.standard: Work out which of the two meanings the sentence intends, then pick the form tied to that meaning.
q-nn-doublemeaning.fast: Garments = clothes; pieces of fabric = cloths. Members of a group = brethren; sons of the same parents = brothers. Algebra signs = indices; tables of contents = indexes.
q-nn-doublemeaning.eliminate: Drop the form that belongs to the other meaning.
traps: Using 'cloths' for garments, or 'clothes' for fabric by the yard.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The officer gave us / several useful informations / about the scheme / before we applied.
practice.why: 'Information' is uncountable, so it has no plural: 'several useful pieces of information' or simply 'useful information'.

a.note: 'The officer gave us' is a correct main clause.

c.note: 'About the scheme' is a correct prepositional phrase.

d.note: 'Before we applied' is a correct clause of time.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She asked the warden for ___ about the hostel rules.
practice.why: 'Advice' is uncountable: it takes no 'a' and no plural.

a.note: 'An advice' is common in Indian English, but the noun cannot be counted; say 'a piece of advice'.

d.note: 'Some' is fine but 'advices' is still a plural of an uncountable noun.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
They have shifted / all the furnitures / to the new office / on the third floor.
practice.why: 'Furniture' is uncountable, so it should be 'all the furniture'.

a.note: 'They have shifted' is a correct present perfect verb.

c.note: 'To the new office' is a correct prepositional phrase.

d.note: 'On the third floor' is a correct phrase of place.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The news from the border ___ reassuring.
practice.why: 'News' ends in -s but is singular, so it takes a singular verb.

a.note: 'The news are' treats the -s as a plural ending; 'news' is singular.

c.note: 'Were' is plural as well as past.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural; the singular would be 'has been'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Mathematics ___ never been his strong subject.
practice.why: 'Mathematics' is the name of one subject and takes a singular verb.

a.note: 'Have' treats the -s as a plural ending.

c.note: 'Are' is plural and also the wrong tense for 'never been'.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
He bought [[a new scissor]] from the stationery shop.
practice.why: 'Scissors' has no singular, so one object is 'a pair of scissors'.

b.note: 'A scissor' invents a singular for a noun that has none.

c.note: Dropping the article leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

d.note: 'A new scissors' puts a singular article before a plural noun.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The state announced / a five-years plan / for the repair / of village roads.
practice.why: A measure used as an adjective before a noun stays singular: 'a five-year plan'.

a.note: 'The state announced' is a correct main clause.

c.note: 'For the repair' is a correct prepositional phrase.

d.note: 'Of village roads' correctly completes the phrase.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
He finished [[a day work]] before noon.
practice.why: Time takes the apostrophe and s: a day's work.

b.note: The apostrophe has simply been dropped.

c.note: This mixes the of-form and the apostrophe together.

d.note: 'A days work' puts the plural -s where the possessive apostrophe belongs.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The warden inspected the ___ hostel after the complaint.
practice.why: A plural already ending in -s takes only the apostrophe: the boys' hostel.

a.note: 'Boys's' adds an s after a plural that already ends in one.

c.note: 'Boy's' would mean a hostel belonging to one boy.

d.note: Without an apostrophe there is no possessive at all.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
They repaired [[the house's roof]] before the monsoon.
practice.why: A lifeless thing normally takes the of-form rather than the apostrophe.

b.note: The apostrophe is used for people, animals and time, not usually for a building.

c.note: 'Houses roof' has neither an apostrophe nor an of-phrase.

d.note: This uses both forms at once.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The park was built with ___ safety in mind.
practice.why: 'Children' is a plural that does not end in -s, so it takes 's.

a.note: 'Childrens' has no apostrophe and is not a word.

c.note: 'Childrens'' adds a plural -s to a noun that is already plural.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The porter carried / all our luggages / up the stairs / without a word.
practice.why: 'Luggage' is uncountable, so it should be 'all our luggage'.

a.note: 'The porter carried' is a correct main clause.

c.note: 'Up the stairs' is a correct phrase of direction.

d.note: 'Without a word' is a correct prepositional phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Punctuality is one important ___ for this promotion.
practice.why: For a single standard, the singular borrowed form is 'criterion'; 'criteria' is its plural.

a.note: 'Criteria' is the plural; the sentence names only one standard, punctuality.

c.note: 'Criterions' adds an ordinary English plural to a word that keeps its Greek plural, 'criteria'.

d.note: 'Criterias' is not a recognised form at all.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The manager put forward / a number of criterions / for shortlisting the candidates / at the final interview.
practice.why: 'A number of' needs a plural noun, and the correct plural of 'criterion' is 'criteria', not 'criterions'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The committee is still collecting ___ before it draws any conclusion.
practice.why: 'Data' is already the plural of 'datum' and is the normal word for a body of facts; it does not take an extra -s.

a.note: 'Datas' adds an ordinary plural -s to a word that is already plural.

c.note: 'A datum' names one single fact, not the body of facts the sentence means.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The country is facing a severe economic [[crisises]] this year.
practice.why: 'This year' and the singular article 'a' both call for the singular form 'crisis'; 'crises' is its plural.

b.note: 'Crises' is the plural form, but the sentence names one crisis, this year's.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
All the ___ of this religious order live together in that monastery.
practice.why: 'Members of a religious or social community' is the sense of 'brethren', not 'brothers' (sons of the same parents).

a.note: 'Brothers' means sons of the same parents, which is not what 'this religious order' describes.

c.note: A singular possessive does not fit a plural count of members.

d.note: A plural possessive needs a following noun, which is missing here.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The old trunk in the attic is full of torn ___ used for dusting furniture.
practice.why: Pieces or scraps of fabric, as opposed to garments, are 'cloths'.

a.note: 'Clothes' means garments worn by people, not scraps of fabric used for dusting.

c.note: A possessive form does not fit a plain plural count.

d.note: 'Clothe' is a verb, not the noun this sentence needs.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
In algebra, / the small numbers written above a variable / are called indexes, / not exponents.
options: the small numbers written above a variable
practice.why: Signs used in algebra are called 'indices', not 'indexes'; 'indexes' are the tables of contents found in books.
